analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generic and biosimilar drugs on the same terms as brand-name drugs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Medicare drug-pricing bill with five cosponsors was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's private drug plans sometimes leave cheaper generic versions off their lists of covered drugs, or charge patients more for them and require extra permission steps, because brand-name drug makers pay plans and their pharmacy-benefit middlemen rebates for preferred placement. This bill would require plans that cover a brand-name drug to also cover any cheaper generic version, without extra hurdles that do not apply to the brand drug. It would also require plans to put generics in a cheaper cost-sharing tier, at least $20 less than the cheapest brand-drug tier.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who take brand-name drugs that have a cheaper generic or biosimilar alternative. They would be guaranteed access to the cheaper version without prior authorization, step therapy, or higher cost-sharing than the brand drug, and generics would get a dedicated cost-sharing tier at least $20 cheaper than the cheapest brand tier.

how_it_helps.text: Plans that cover a brand-name drug must also cover every cheaper generic version of it, and at least one cheaper biosimilar of any covered reference biological product, on their formulary.

Plans may not impose prior authorization, utilization management, or step therapy on a required generic or biosimilar that is more restrictive than what the brand-name drug faces, and cannot give the brand drug preferred status over it.

Plans using cost-sharing tiers must create a tier only for generics and biosimilars, with either no cost-sharing or a copay at least $20 below the cheapest brand-drug tier, and a second specialty tier for high-cost generics priced at least 5 percentage points below other specialty tiers.
The requirements take effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, with the Secretary of Health and Human Services setting uniform implementation rules and quarterly updates.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose sales and rebate leverage when cheaper versions must get equal or better placement. Medicare drug plans would lose flexibility to steer patients to high-rebate brand drugs, which they currently use to keep premiums down, so some of the cost could shift into premiums. HHS would take on quarterly implementation work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and drug plans

drawbacks.text: Part D plans currently negotiate large rebates from brand-name manufacturers in exchange for preferred placement, and use that rebate revenue to keep premiums low. Forcing generics into preferred positions could shrink rebate revenue and push some plans to raise premiums or trim benefits elsewhere to compensate.

The bill relies on the Secretary to set uniform determinations and implementation rules on a quarterly schedule, a significant ongoing administrative task; plans would face compliance costs in reworking formularies and benefit designs.

The bill does nothing about the underlying rebate system that rewards keeping cheap drugs off formularies, so it treats a symptom rather than the cause, and its protections apply mainly to drugs that already have a competing generic or biosimilar on the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: seniors taking drugs with an available cheaper copy would pay less and face fewer hoops. The main risk is modest premium pressure on plans that now rely on brand-drug rebates. The design is workable but partial; it would not change the rebate incentives that caused the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, for himself and Senator Menendez, a bipartisan pairing.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Five senators cosponsored the bill: three Democrats and two Republicans.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare drug plans and pharmacy-benefit managers keep their current formulary freedom, and brand-name drug makers keep the rebate-driven sales that cheaper alternatives would have displaced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug plans and brand-name drug makers

for.name: James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a Democratic co-lead.

for.name: Bob Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (co-lead cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic co-lead.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; it sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: a Republican sponsor and lead Democratic cosponsor, with the bill's five cosponsors split three Democrats and two Republicans; no opposition was ever recorded, because no committee or floor vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and their pharmacy-benefit managers
industries.note: These plans currently profit from rebates that brand-name drug makers pay for preferred formulary placement, and steer patients to high-rebate brands even when cheaper generics exist. The bill would bar that steering and cap what plans can charge for generics, shrinking their flexibility and rebate revenue.

Whenever a generic or biosimilar of their drug exists, it would have to appear on formularies with equal access and a cost-sharing tier at least $20 cheaper, directly cutting into brand-drug sales that the rebate system currently protects.

Their products would be guaranteed formulary inclusion and preferred, lower-cost-sharing tiers whenever they are cheaper than the brand-name original, expanding their market at the direct expense of brand-drug sales.
